hints: Start by thinking about the difference between a protein taken from a cow or pig pancreas and one made from the human gene - how similar is the amino acid sequence to your own insulin?
Think about what happens when the immune system meets a slightly foreign protein, and what that means for allergies, effectiveness and long-term use.
Now think about supply - how many animal pancreases would be needed to treat millions of diabetics, compared with bacteria dividing every 20 minutes in a fermenter?
Finish by linking safety and acceptability - risk of animal pathogens, cost of purification, and ethical or religious concerns about animal products.
walkthrough:
Why exact human sequence matters**
Animal insulin differs by one or a few amino acids from human insulin. Your immune system can recognise that tiny difference as foreign and make antibodies against it. Recombinant bacteria carry the exact human gene, so they make protein identical to your own.

No rejection means safer and more effective treatment**
Because it is identical, there is much less chance of allergy, immune attack or side effects. It also binds human receptors properly, so it works faster and better, and patients do not develop tolerance as they sometimes did with animal insulin.

Supply, safety and cost**
Animal pancreases are limited and variable - huge numbers are needed for one patient. Transformed bacteria can be grown in unlimited amounts in fermenters, giving a pure, consistent supply at lower cost, with no risk of co-purified animal viruses or pathogens.

Acceptability**
Many people object to using animal tissues for ethical, vegetarian or religious reasons. Making the human protein in microbes avoids killing animals and removes those objections.

Final answer: Any four: product identical to human insulin; no immune response / allergic reaction / side effects; higher activity / more rapid response; no tolerance develops; no risk of transmitting animal diseases; unlimited / large-scale supply; lower production cost; no ethical / religious objections.

hints: Go column by column through Fig. 3.1 from position 1 to 32 and tick every position where human and salmon have exactly the same three-letter code.
Think about the formula for a percentage: (number the same divided by total in one sequence) x 100 - what is the total length here?
walkthrough:
Count identical positions**
Compare like with like at each position. For example 1 Cys = Cys, 2 Gly vs Ser different, 3 Asn = Asn, and so on. If you work carefully through all 32 positions you find 16 matches at positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 14, 18, 21, 23, 25, 28, 30, 32.

Convert to percentage**
Total amino acids in one calcitonin = 32. Use: $$\text{similarity} = \frac{\text{number identical}}{\text{total}} \times 100 = \frac{16}{32} \times 100 = 50\%$$
Final answer: Working: $(16 / 32) \times 100$; Answer: $50$ %.

hints: Recall what bioinformatics actually stores - huge libraries of DNA, amino acid and protein shape data collected from all over the world.
Think how you could use that library starting from human calcitonin to hunt for a better version that still does the same job.
walkthrough:
A searchable library of life**
Bioinformatics is not just computers - it is curated databases holding millions of DNA and amino acid sequences plus protein structures, pooled from labs worldwide.

Finding salmon calcitonin by similarity**
The human calcitonin sequence can be used as a query to search the database for similar sequences in other species. Salmon calcitonin showed about 50% identity, enough to have the same basic function, and modelling could predict it would still fit the human calcitonin receptor, but with higher activity and longer life.

Final answer: Bioinformatics provides databases of base / amino acid / protein sequence data for comparison; sequences similar to human calcitonin were searched for / identified; allows modelling / predicting of 3D / tertiary structure and receptor binding.

hints: Think of the two opposite jobs in making recombinant DNA - one tool to open the plasmid circle, another tool to glue the new gene in.
Remember which enzyme cuts at specific recognition sequences to leave sticky ends, and which enzyme seals sugar-phosphate backbones and phosphodiester bonds.
walkthrough:
Cutting open the vector**
A restriction endonuclease cuts double-stranded DNA at a specific recognition sequence, opening the plasmid and also cutting out the salmon calcitonin gene with matching sticky ends.

Joining to make recombinant plasmid**
DNA ligase then catalyses formation of phosphodiester bonds between the gene and plasmid backbones, sealing the new gene permanently into the circle.
Final answer: Cut plasmid DNA: restriction enzyme / restriction endonuclease; Join gene to plasmid DNA: DNA ligase.

hints: Picture a plasmid inside E. coli - what about its size, shape and ability to copy itself makes it easy to get into cells and make many copies?
Now think about the genetic tools built into a vector - how do you insert a gene at a precise place and then prove which bacteria took it up?
walkthrough:
Easy to handle and multiply**
Plasmids are small, circular DNA molecules separate from the chromosome. Small size lets them enter bacteria easily and resist damage, and an origin of replication lets them replicate independently and rapidly to give many copies of the inserted gene per cell.

Designed for cloning and selection**
Vectors contain single restriction sites or a multiple cloning site, so restriction enzymes cut once and the new gene can be ligated in without disrupting replication. They also carry marker genes, such as antibiotic resistance, so only transformed bacteria with the plasmid survive and can be recognised.

Final answer: Any two explained: small so easily taken up by cells; replicates independently / has origin of replication so high copy number; has restriction sites / multiple cloning site so gene can be inserted; has marker / antibiotic resistance genes so recombinants can be identified; circular so stable.

hints: Remember how transcription starts - RNA polymerase must bind to a promoter just before the gene. Are bacterial and human promoters built the same way?
Think what happens if you put a eukaryotic promoter into E. coli - will its RNA polymerase plus transcription factors recognise it and make mRNA?
walkthrough:
Promoters are species-specific landing pads**
Transcription only starts when RNA polymerase binds the promoter. Bacterial promoters, e.g. lac, have -10 and -35 sequences recognised by bacterial sigma factors, while eukaryotic promoters have TATA boxes, enhancers and need many transcription factors. The sequences and proteins are different.

No recognition means no expression**
If the salmon (eukaryotic) gene keeps its own promoter, E. coli RNA polymerase will not bind to it, so no mRNA is made and no calcitonin is produced. An expression vector therefore places the gene downstream of a prokaryotic promoter that bacterial polymerase does recognise, switching transcription on.

Final answer: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic promoter sequences are different / RNA polymerases are different; prokaryotic RNA polymerase does not recognise / bind eukaryotic promoter; so no transcription / mRNA / gene expression without prokaryotic promoter; eukaryotic promoters need transcription factors absent in bacteria.
